title: Seasonal constellations
keyIdea: A constellation is a pattern of stars. The stars stay where they are, but Earth goes round the Sun once a year, so its night side faces a different part of space in each season. In the north of the world, Orion fills winter nights, Leo spring nights, Scorpius summer nights and Pegasus autumn nights. A constellation we cannot see is not gone: it is in the day sky, near the Sun, where the bright sky hides it. Stars rise about 4 minutes earlier each night, about 2 hours a month. Constellations close to the North Star, like the Plough and Cassiopeia, never set from Britain, so we see them all year.
familyTip: On a clear evening, go out at the same time once a month and look south from the same spot. Draw where Orion (in winter) or the brightest pattern you can find sits above a tree or roof. Month by month it slides west and a new pattern rises in the east. Then turn north: the Plough is still there, just turned round the North Star.

visual.caption: In the north of the world, which constellations fill winter nights and which fill summer nights? Drag each one into a box, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: move Earth round the Sun, find the stars hidden by daylight, sort the seasons, track Orion and find the ones that never set.

kid: A constellation is a pattern of stars, like Orion the hunter or Leo the lion. The stars in it are very far away. They keep the same pattern for our whole life.

Earth goes round the Sun once a year. At night we look out from the side of Earth that faces away from the Sun. As Earth moves, that night side faces a new part of space. So each season has its own constellations.

In the north of the world, Orion is high on winter nights. Leo comes in spring, Scorpius in summer and Pegasus in autumn. In summer Orion is still there, but it is in the day sky near the Sun. The bright sky hides it.

Stars rise about 4 minutes earlier each night. After a month that is about 2 hours. So at bedtime a pattern sits a little further west each week. A few patterns near the North Star, like the Plough, never set from Britain. We can see them all year.
adult: Ages 9 to 10. This meets NGSS 5-ESS1-2: show patterns in the night sky, including stars that are only seen in some seasons. It builds on Year 5 Earth and space in the English National Curriculum, where Earth goes round the Sun. Key words: constellation, orbit, night side, seasonal, circumpolar, North Star (Polaris), rise, set, due south.

At night we see the half of the sky that faces away from the Sun. A constellation is best placed when Earth is between it and the Sun. It is lost in daylight when the Sun is in front of it: Orion from about May to July, Leo around August. The lab shows the sky at midnight, with each pattern in its real direction. In the evening, each one is best a month or two later. Earth moves about 1 degree along its orbit each day. So a star comes back to the same place about 4 minutes earlier each night, or 2 hours a month. Lab times are for Britain, without summer time. Scorpius is low in the south from Britain. Nearer the equator it stands higher.

Common mistakes: thinking stars switch off or leave in summer; thinking the patterns travel round space; and blaming clouds or Earth's tilt. The tilt gives hot and cold seasons, but where Earth is on its orbit sets which stars fill the night. Some children think stars vanish in the day; they are only outshone. Not every pattern is seasonal: from Britain the Plough and Cassiopeia never set. And the south does not see the same stars in the same season: there, December is summer, and Orion looks upside down.

In the lab your child moves Earth round the Sun and finds when each of four patterns is high at midnight. They tap the one hidden behind the Sun in June, September and December, and sort the four into seasons. They step through the months at 9 pm: Orion rises in the east in November, is due south in January and sets in the west in April. Last, they find the Plough and Cassiopeia turning round the North Star in every season.

practice.prompt: Seasonal constellations: why do we see different constellations in winter and in summer?
choices: Earth's night side faces a different part of space
The stars move to new places
Some stars switch off in summer
practice.hint: Think about what you moved round the Sun in the lab.
practice.explain: The stars stay put. As Earth goes round the Sun, its night side faces a different part of space each season.

practice.prompt: A star rises about 4 minutes earlier each night. How many minutes earlier will it rise after {a} nights?
practice.hint: Multiply the number of nights by 4 minutes.
practice.explain: {a} × 4 = {=4*a} minutes earlier. Over a month of about 30 nights that adds up to about 2 hours.

practice.prompt: A constellation is due south at {a} pm tonight. Each month it is due south about 2 hours earlier. At about what time pm will it be due south one month from now?
practice.hint: Take 2 hours off the time tonight.
practice.explain: {a} pm − 2 hours = about {=a-2} pm. Stars come round about 4 minutes earlier each night, which is about 2 hours a month.

practice.prompt: In June, where are the stars of Orion?
choices: In the day sky, near the Sun
practice.hint: In the lab, which constellation was behind the Sun in June?
practice.explain: Orion is still there in June, but it is up in the daytime near the Sun, so the bright sky hides it.

practice.prompt: From Britain, which constellation can you see on clear nights all year?
practice.hint: Which patterns circled the North Star in the lab?
practice.explain: The Plough is close to the North Star, so it circles it and never sets from Britain. Orion and Scorpius are seasonal.

choices: A cloud of gas round the Sun
pool.hint: Orion, Leo and the Plough are all examples.
pool.explain: A constellation is a pattern of stars, such as Orion or Leo. Its stars are very far away and keep the same pattern.

pool.prompt: In the north of the world, which constellation is high on winter nights?
pool.hint: Which one did you put in the winter box?
pool.explain: Orion is the great winter constellation in the north of the world. Scorpius is a summer one and Pegasus an autumn one.

pool.prompt: Why can't we see stars in the daytime?
choices: They go out in the day
pool.hint: Stars are still there behind the blue sky.
pool.explain: Stars are in the sky in the day too, but sunlight lights up the air so brightly that we cannot see them.

pool.prompt: Stars rise about 2 hours earlier each month. How many hours earlier will a star rise after {a} months?
pool.explain: {a} × 2 = {=2*a} hours earlier. That is why a winter pattern has left the evening sky by summer.

pool.prompt: What does Earth's tilt change, and what does its orbit change?
choices: Tilt: hot and cold seasons. Orbit: which stars fill the night
Tilt: which stars we see. Orbit: nothing
pool.hint: Which one did the lab use to move the night side round?
pool.explain: The tilt gives us summer and winter weather. The trip round the Sun turns our night side to a new part of space.

pool.prompt: In December it is summer in Australia. Which constellation is in their December night sky?
pool.hint: Earth's night side faces the same way for everyone on that date.
pool.explain: In December the night side faces Orion for the whole Earth. In Australia that is summer, and Orion looks upside down to them.

pool.prompt: Earth goes about 30 degrees round its orbit each month. How many degrees does it go in {a} months?
pool.hint: Multiply 30 degrees by the number of months.
pool.explain: {a} × 30 = {=30*a} degrees. After 6 months Earth is on the far side of the Sun and the night side faces the opposite way.

pool.prompt: Why does the Plough never set when seen from Britain?
choices: It is close to the North Star, so it circles it
pool.hint: Watch where the Plough went in each season in the lab.
pool.explain: The Plough is near the North Star. From Britain it circles the North Star and stays above the horizon all night, all year.

pool.prompt: Orion is due south at 10 pm on 15 January. At 10 pm on 15 February, where is it?
pool.hint: Stars come round earlier each night, so at the same clock time they have moved on.
pool.explain: By February Orion reaches due south about 2 hours earlier, at about 8 pm, so at 10 pm it has moved on to the west.
